# Tests of the caching of go test's analysis (GOEXPERIMENT=vetfiles),
# whose results are cached per (package, analyzer). Each line of -x
# output that runs the tool on an analysis.cfg file analyzes one
# package; we count them to see which packages were re-analyzed.
#
# The cache is shared with other tests, so counts are checked only
# after a run that has populated it with the results of the standard
# library.

[short] skip 'builds and runs an analysis tool'
[!compiler:gc] skip

env GOEXPERIMENT=vetfiles

# a calls the printf wrapper lib.Logf with a bad argument. printf
# learns that Logf is a wrapper from a fact about lib, so it reports
# the call in a. lib's own diagnostic is not reported, as lib is not
# a root package.
! go test ./a
stderr 'a.go:10:12: example.com/cache/lib.Logf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
! stderr 'lib.go'

# A second run uses cached results: the tool analyzes no packages,
# and its metadata query is not executed. The cached diagnostic is
# reported again.
! go test -x ./a
stderr 'a.go:10:12: example.com/cache/lib.Logf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
! stderr 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'
! stderr 'analysistool.* -describe='

# A change to lib that preserves its types and facts re-analyzes lib
# but not a (early cutoff).
cp lib_body.go.txt lib/lib.go
! go test -x ./a
stderr 'a.go:10:12: example.com/cache/lib.Logf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
stderr -count=1 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'

# A change to lib that preserves its types but changes its facts
# (Logf is no longer a printf wrapper) re-analyzes both lib and a, and
# the diagnostic goes away.
cp lib_nowrap.go.txt lib/lib.go
go test -x ./a
stdout '^ok\s+example.com/cache/a'
! stderr 'Logf format'
stderr -count=2 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'

# Restoring lib restores the facts on which a's earlier results were
# keyed, so both are found in the cache.
cp lib.go.txt lib/lib.go
! go test -x ./a
stderr 'a.go:10:12: example.com/cache/lib.Logf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
! stderr 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'

# lib was analyzed above by printf only for its facts, as a dependency
# of a, so its diagnostics were not computed. Vetting lib itself with
# printf, whose diagnostics are reported, re-analyzes lib (but not a)
# and reports them. (lib's test is external, so the root package is
# lib itself, not a variant of it; the other package analyzed is
# lib_test.) The facts of lib's results are unchanged, so a's results
# remain valid, and vetting both analyzes nothing.
! go test -x -vet=printf ./lib
stderr 'lib.go:10:41: fmt.Sprintf format %d has arg "lib" of wrong type string'
stderr -count=2 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'
! go test -x -vet=printf ./a ./lib
stderr 'a.go:10:12: example.com/cache/lib.Logf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
stderr 'lib.go:10:41: fmt.Sprintf format %d has arg "lib" of wrong type string'
! stderr 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'

# Results are cached per analyzer: printf alone, a subset of the
# default analyzers, is found in the cache.
! go test -x -vet=printf ./a
stderr 'a.go:10:12: example.com/cache/lib.Logf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
! stderr 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'

# Adding unusedresult, which is not among the defaults, re-analyzes a.
# unusedresult uses no facts, so lib need not be re-analyzed.
! go test -x -vet=printf,unusedresult ./a
stderr 'a.go:10:12: example.com/cache/lib.Logf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
stderr 'a.go:11:2: result of fmt.Sprint call not used'
stderr -count=1 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'
! go test -x -vet=printf,unusedresult ./a
stderr 'a.go:11:2: result of fmt.Sprint call not used'
! stderr 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'

# The build configuration is among the inputs: a build tag that adds a
# file to a yields its diagnostics, and removing the tag drops them.
! go test -tags=extra ./a
stderr 'extra.go:7:39: fmt.Sprintf format %s has arg 1 of wrong type int'
! go test ./a
! stderr 'extra.go'

# The target configuration is among the inputs: the same file yields a
# shift diagnostic only where uint has 32 bits. (The tool is built for
# the target and runs on the host, so this requires a host that can
# run 386 executables. The package also has a printf diagnostic, so
# that the analysis fails and the test binary does not run.)
# Both GOARCH values are set explicitly, as the default GOARCH may be
# 32-bit (e.g. on the linux-386 builders, which set GOARCH=386).
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] env oldGOARCH=$GOARCH
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] env GOARCH=386
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] ! go test -vet=printf,shift ./shift
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] stderr 'shift.go:7:24: x \(32 bits\) too small for shift of 40'
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] stderr 'shift.go:9:39: fmt.Sprintf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] env GOARCH=amd64
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] ! go test -vet=printf,shift ./shift
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] ! stderr 'too small for shift'
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] stderr 'shift.go:9:39: fmt.Sprintf format %d has arg "x" of wrong type string'
[GOOS:linux] [GOARCH:amd64] env GOARCH=$oldGOARCH

# The key of a pass includes the facts of every analyzer in the
# Requires closure, not just those of the analyzer itself. lostcancel
# uses no facts, but its prerequisite ctrlflow does: a fact that
# exit.Fatal never returns makes the return statement after the call
# to it unreachable, so c's cancel function is used on all paths. A
# change to exit that preserves its types but not that fact
# re-analyzes exit and c, yielding a diagnostic; restoring exit
# analyzes nothing.
go test -vet=lostcancel ./c
cp exit_returns.go.txt exit/exit.go
! go test -x -vet=lostcancel ./c
stderr 'c.go:10:2: the cancel function is not used on all paths \(possible context leak\)'
stderr -count=2 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'
cp exit.go.txt exit/exit.go
go test -x -vet=lostcancel ./c
! stderr 'possible context leak'
! stderr 'analysistool.* .*analysis\.cfg'

# TODO: test these aspects of the identity of an analyzer once custom
# analyzers can be configured (go.vet files outside std):
#   - An edit to a package imported, directly or indirectly, by the
#     package of a variable from which an analyzer is reachable
#     invalidates that analyzer's results, but not those of analyzers
#     reachable only from other variables.
#   - An analyzer declared in one package whose Run function is in
#     another (for example, a shared Run function configured by the
#     analyzer's fields): an edit to the declaring package invalidates
#     its results.
#   - An analyzer reachable from different sets of variables in
#     different invocations (for example, named directly in one and
#     as a suite member in another) has a different identity in each:
#     results are correct but not shared between them.
#   - Which analyzers, not just which packages, were re-analyzed: for
#     example, that an edit to one analyzer leaves the results of
#     another on the same package cached. (Counting the tool's
#     executions observes only packages.)

-- go.mod --
module example.com/cache

go 1.28
-- lib/lib.go --
package lib

import "fmt"

// Logf is a printf wrapper.
func Logf(format string, args ...any) { fmt.Printf(format, args...) }

func helper() int { return 1 }

func bad() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%d", "lib") }
-- lib.go.txt --
package lib

import "fmt"

// Logf is a printf wrapper.
func Logf(format string, args ...any) { fmt.Printf(format, args...) }

func helper() int { return 1 }

func bad() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%d", "lib") }
-- lib_body.go.txt --
package lib

import "fmt"

// Logf is a printf wrapper.
func Logf(format string, args ...any) { fmt.Printf(format, args...) }

func helper() int { return 2 }

func bad() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%d", "lib") }
-- lib_nowrap.go.txt --
package lib

import "fmt"

// Logf is not a printf wrapper.
func Logf(format string, args ...any) { fmt.Println(format, args) }

func helper() int { return 1 }

func bad() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%d", "lib") }
-- lib/lib_test.go --
package lib_test

import "testing"

func TestLib(t *testing.T) {}
-- a/a.go --
package a

import (
	"fmt"

	"example.com/cache/lib"
)

func F() {
	lib.Logf("%d", "x")
	fmt.Sprint("y")
}
-- a/extra.go --
//go:build extra

package a

import "fmt"

func G() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%s", 1) }
-- shift/shift.go --
package shift

import "fmt"

var x uint

func F() uint { return x << 40 }

func G() string { return fmt.Sprintf("%d", "x") }
-- shift/shift_test.go --
package shift

import "testing"

func TestF(t *testing.T) {}
-- exit/exit.go --
package exit

import "os"

// Fatal does not return.
func Fatal() { os.Exit(1) }
-- exit.go.txt --
package exit

import "os"

// Fatal does not return.
func Fatal() { os.Exit(1) }
-- exit_returns.go.txt --
package exit

import "os"

// Fatal returns.
func Fatal() { _ = os.Args }
-- c/c.go --
package c

import (
	"context"

	"example.com/cache/exit"
)

func F(ok bool) {
	ctx, cancel := context.WithCancel(context.Background())
	if !ok {
		exit.Fatal()
		return
	}
	defer cancel()
	_ = ctx
}
-- c/c_test.go --
package c

import "testing"

func TestF(t *testing.T) {}
-- a/a_test.go --
package a

import "testing"

func TestF(t *testing.T) {}
